fuente.nota: Texto recortado por párrafos; sin cambios en las frases.

parrafos: Inflation means that the general level of prices is going up. More money will be needed to pay for goods (like a loaf of bread) and services (like getting a haircut at the hairdresser's). Economists measure inflation regularly to know an economy's state. Inflation changes the ratio of money towards goods or services; more money is needed to get the same amount of a good or service, or the same amount of money will get a lower amount of a good or service. Economists defined certain customer baskets to be able to measure inflation. There can be positive and negative effects. The opposite of inflation is deflation.

When the total money in an economy (the money supply) increases too rapidly, the quality of the money (the currency value) often decreases. Economists generally think that the increased money supply (monetary inflation) causes the price of goods/services to increase (price inflation) over a longer period. They disagree on causes over a shorter period.

Demand-pull inflation says that inflation is the result of "too much money chasing too few goods." In other words, if the need for buying goods is growing faster than the amount of goods that have been made, prices will go up. This is most likely to happen in economies that are growing fast.

Whenever a product is bought or sold beyond its real price that it is worth, inflation of money happens. For example, if a company makes a small amount of goods and a lot of people buy them, then the company will higher the prices of these goods.

The cost-push inflation theory says that when the cost of making goods (which are paid by the company) go up, people make prices higher, because they want to make a profit from selling that product. The higher costs of making goods can include things like workers' wages, taxes to be paid to the government, or higher costs of raw materials from other countries.
However, Austrian School economists think this is wrong, because if people have to pay higher prices, this just means they have less to spend on other things.

Almost everyone thinks excessive inflation is bad. Inflation affects different people in different ways. It also depends on whether inflation is expected or not. If the inflation rate is equal to what most people are expecting (anticipated inflation), then we can adjust and the cost is not as high. For example, banks can change their interest rates and workers can negotiate contracts that include automatic wage hikes as the price level goes up.
Creditors lose and debtors gain if the lender does not guess inflation correctly. For those who borrow, this is similar to getting an interest-free loan.
resumen_es: Define la inflación y cómo se mide, expone sus causas (exceso de dinero, inflación de demanda y de costes, con la crítica de la escuela austriaca) y sus costes, según sea o no anticipada.

ideas_clave.idea: Inflation is a general rise in prices that reduces what a given sum of money can buy; economists track it with consumer baskets, and its opposite is deflation.
Economists broadly agree that an excessive expansion of the money supply drives prices up in the long run, but they differ about short-term causes.
According to the demand-pull view, prices rise when spending grows faster than output, which tends to happen in fast-growing economies.
The cost-push theory blames higher production costs, such as wages, taxes or imported inputs, passed on to consumers, an explanation rejected by the Austrian School.
Excessive inflation is widely regarded as harmful, although expected inflation is less costly because banks and workers can adapt rates and wage contracts.
Unexpected inflation redistributes wealth from lenders to borrowers, who effectively enjoy an interest-free loan.

resumen_modelo: The text defines inflation as a general rise in prices, which means that more money is needed to buy the same goods and services; it is measured through consumer baskets, and its opposite is deflation. Economists broadly agree that excessive monetary growth raises prices in the long run, but short-term explanations differ. Demand-pull inflation arises when spending outpaces production, typically in booming economies, whereas cost-push inflation occurs when firms pass on higher wages, taxes or import costs, a view the Austrian School rejects. Finally, anticipated inflation is less harmful, since rates and wages can adjust, while unexpected inflation favours debtors over creditors.

preguntas.pregunta: In which kind of economy is demand-pull inflation most likely?
opciones: In economies that are growing fast
In economies that import most raw materials
respuestas: In economies that are growing fast
preguntas.cita: This is most likely to happen in economies that are growing fast.
preguntas.explicacion: La inflación de demanda aparece sobre todo en economías que crecen deprisa. Las materias primas importadas y los impuestos se asocian en el texto a la inflación de costes.

preguntas.pregunta: Which of the following is NOT mentioned as a production cost in the cost-push theory?
preguntas.cita: The higher costs of making goods can include things like workers' wages, taxes to be paid to the government, or higher costs of raw materials from other countries.
preguntas.explicacion: El texto cita salarios, impuestos y materias primas importadas; la publicidad no aparece.

preguntas.enunciado: Indica si la afirmación es verdadera (V), falsa (F) o no se dice (ND).
preguntas.pregunta: Austrian School economists accept the cost-push theory of inflation.
preguntas.cita: However, Austrian School economists think this is wrong
preguntas.explicacion: La escuela austriaca rechaza la teoría de la inflación de costes: si se pagan precios más altos, se gasta menos en otras cosas.

preguntas.pregunta: Why do Austrian School economists reject the cost-push explanation?
respuestas: Because if consumers pay more for some products they have less money left for other goods, so higher costs change relative prices but do not raise the general price level.
preguntas.cita: if people have to pay higher prices, this just means they have less to spend on other things
preguntas.explicacion: Es una inferencia: el argumento implica que el gasto total no aumenta, solo se redistribuye, de modo que no hay subida general de precios.

preguntas.enunciado: Busca en el párrafo 6 una palabra que signifique «subidas» (de salario).
preguntas.cita: workers can negotiate contracts that include automatic wage hikes as the price level goes up
preguntas.explicacion: «Hikes» significa subidas, sobre todo en precios, tipos o salarios (wage hikes, rate hikes).

preguntas.pregunta: Why does unexpected inflation favour borrowers over lenders?
respuestas: Because borrowers repay their debts with money that has lost value, while the interest rate fixed by the lender did not take that inflation into account; for the borrower it is like an interest-free loan.
preguntas.cita: Creditors lose and debtors gain if the lender does not guess inflation correctly.
preguntas.explicacion: La inflación no anticipada reduce el valor real de la deuda; el acreedor recibe menos poder adquisitivo del que esperaba.
